stem: A team stores a `session_id` in their database after a user's first message and, on the next request, sends only the new message plus that `session_id`, assuming Claude will look up and remember the earlier conversation on its own. The agent responds as if it has no memory of the earlier exchange. What's the misunderstanding?
explanation: A session_id is the application's own database lookup key for retrieving stored history — it is not something the model itself remembers. The model only ever sees what's actually in the request body; the full conversation history and system prompt must be sent on every request, since there's no server-side memory between calls.

choices.text: session_id is only the application's own lookup key for stored history — the model has no awareness of it; the actual conversation history must be resent in the request body every time
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is a directly documented gotcha — a session_id finds stored history in your database; that history still has to be sent in the request for the model to have any awareness of it.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; session_id is supposed to let Claude retrieve the conversation automatically on the server side
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is exactly the misconception being tested — there's no server-side memory the model can pull from using a session_id; the app must resend the history itself.

choices.text: The issue is that the session_id format was invalid
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: even a validly-formatted session_id wouldn't give the model access to prior history on its own — the model only sees what's included in the request body.

choices.text: The issue is that the model's context window was too small to hold the session_id
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: session_id is a tiny identifier and isn't a context-capacity issue — the actual problem is that the conversation history itself was never included in the request.

choices.text: The issue is that the request didn't include a system prompt, unrelated to session_id
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: while the system prompt must also be resent every request, the specific misunderstanding described here is about session_id not carrying memory on its own, regardless of the system prompt.

choices.text: The issue is that session_id only works with the Batch API, not real-time
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: session_id as an application-level lookup key isn't tied to a specific API mode — the core misunderstanding is about statelessness generally.

stem: A team notices their per-request cost and latency both climb steadily as a customer's support conversation grows longer, even though each individual message is short. What explains this, per the stateless core principle?
explanation: The full conversation history and system prompt must be sent on every request — input token cost scales with conversation length, so an unmanaged, ever-growing history gets more expensive (and slower) with every turn, even if each new message itself is short.

choices.text: Input token cost scales with total conversation length since the full history must be resent every request — an ever-growing history gets more expensive and slower with every turn
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented explanation exactly — even short new messages add to a growing total that must be resent in full on each request, driving up cost and latency over time.

choices.text: This is unexpected and indicates a billing bug, since only the newest message should count toward cost
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this contradicts the stateless core principle — the full history is resent and counted every request, not just the newest message, so this is expected behavior, not a bug.

choices.text: This only happens if prompt caching is disabled; enabling caching eliminates any cost growth entirely
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: caching can reduce the cost of resending unchanged content but doesn't eliminate the fundamental relationship between conversation length and total tokens processed as the conversation genuinely grows.

choices.text: This is caused by the model's temperature increasing automatically with longer conversations
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: temperature is a fixed sampling parameter and doesn't automatically change with conversation length — the cost/latency growth is explained by token count, not sampling behavior.

choices.text: This only happens with the Batch API, not real-time requests
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the stateless core principle and its cost implications apply to conversation history generally, regardless of which API mode is used.

choices.text: This is caused by the model needing more time to "remember" more turns internally
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the model has no persistent internal memory between calls — the cost/latency increase is purely a function of the token volume being sent and processed in each request, not internal recall effort.

stem: A long customer conversation is being managed by simply keeping the most recent 20 turns and dropping everything older. Midway through turn 35, the customer references a specific budget figure they mentioned in turn 3, which has since been dropped. The agent has no idea what figure they mean. What strategy was used, and what's its documented weakness?
explanation: This is the sliding window strategy — keep the most recent N turns, drop older ones. Its documented weakness is exactly this: it fails when the user references an earlier decision or exact figure that's been dropped, since there's no mechanism preserving specific older facts.

choices.text: Sliding window — its documented weakness is failing when the user references an earlier decision or exact figure that's already been dropped
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented sliding window strategy and its exact stated weakness — losing specific earlier facts that a user later references.

choices.text: Progressive summarization — its documented weakness is that summaries lose precision for exact values
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this scenario describes hard-dropping older turns entirely (a sliding window), not summarizing them — progressive summarization at least attempts to retain some information about older content in summary form.

choices.text: Structured state objects — its documented weakness is only being as good as discipline about updating it
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the scenario describes keeping only the most recent N raw turns and dropping the rest, which is the sliding window pattern, not a structured state object being updated over time.

choices.text: Tool result compression — its documented weakness is requiring knowing in advance what's needed
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: tool result compression applies specifically to verbose tool outputs, not to general conversational turn history, which is what's being dropped here.

choices.text: Persistent reference sections — its documented weakness is needing to be maintained as its own block
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: persistent reference sections are specifically kept exact and separate from general summarization/dropping — the scenario describes the opposite, dropping older turns entirely without any such persistent block.

choices.text: There is no named strategy for this; it's simply a bug
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this matches the documented sliding window strategy exactly, along with its documented weakness — not an unnamed bug.

stem: A travel-planning assistant maintains a JSON object like `{"monthly_budget_max": 4200, "space_type": "private_office", "must_have": ["bike storage"]}`, updated as the conversation evolves and included on every request. What strategy is this, and what's its main weakness?
explanation: This is structured state objects — a JSON object of current, relevant facts, included on every request and updated as things change. Its documented weakness is that it's only as good as the discipline about updating it — if a fact changes but the object isn't updated, stale state persists.

choices.text: Structured state objects — the weakness is that it's only as good as the discipline about actually keeping it updated as things change
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented structured state objects strategy and its exact stated weakness — reliability depends entirely on consistently updating the object as facts change.

choices.text: Sliding window — the weakness is failing when a user references a dropped earlier figure
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the scenario describes a maintained, updated JSON object of current facts, not dropping older raw turns — that's the sliding window pattern, which this isn't.

choices.text: Persistent reference sections — the weakness is needing separate maintenance from general summarization
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: while persistent reference sections are also maintained separately, the specific pattern described (a JSON object of current, relevant, updated facts) matches structured state objects, whose weakness is specifically about update discipline.

choices.text: Progressive summarization — the weakness is losing precision for exact values
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this describes structured, precise state (an exact budget number, specific requirements), not a summarized, potentially imprecise narrative — that's the structured state objects pattern.

choices.text: Tool result compression — the weakness is requiring advance knowledge of what's needed
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: tool result compression is about trimming verbose tool outputs after processing, not about maintaining an evolving fact object across the conversation.

choices.text: There is no documented weakness for this strategy
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the documented weakness for structured state objects is explicitly stated — reliability depends on discipline about updating it.

stem: A legal-assistant system defines certain terms (e.g. "the Agreement," "the Effective Date") at the start of a long negotiation conversation and needs these definitions to remain exact and available throughout, regardless of how much general summarization happens to older turns. What context-shrinking strategy element addresses this specifically?
explanation: Persistent reference sections — story bibles, defined terms, safety info, scale parameters — are kept exact across the whole conversation, separate from general summarization. This is exactly the fit for defined legal terms that must stay precise and available, unlike content that can be safely summarized.

choices.text: Persistent reference sections — kept exact across the whole conversation, separate from general summarization, exactly fitting defined terms that must stay precise
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented persistent reference sections strategy exactly — defined terms are explicitly listed as an example use case, kept exact and separate from general summarization.

choices.text: Sliding window — keeping the most recent N turns automatically preserves defined terms
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: a sliding window would drop the defined terms once they fall outside the recent-N-turns window, which is exactly the weakness this scenario needs to avoid.

choices.text: Tool result compression — stripping unneeded fields from tool output automatically preserves definitions
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: tool result compression addresses verbose tool outputs, not conversational definitions established in the dialogue itself.

choices.text: Progressive summarization alone, without any separate persistent block, is sufficient for exact term preservation
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: progressive summarization's documented weakness is losing precision for exact values — definitions needing to stay exact specifically require the separate persistent reference section, not summarization alone.

choices.text: Structured state objects, updated only when a new definition is introduced and never otherwise maintained
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: while structured state objects can hold facts, the documented strategy specifically suited to exact, persistent definitions kept separate from evolving summarization is persistent reference sections.

choices.text: There is no documented strategy for preserving exact definitions across a long conversation
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: persistent reference sections are explicitly documented for exactly this use case.

stem: A returning user opens a new session the next day to continue apartment-hunting. The application re-embeds the exact search results (listings, prices, availability) from yesterday's session verbatim into the new session's context, to save the cost of a fresh search. What's the risk with this approach?
explanation: For a returning user, re-embedding stale tool output from a prior session is a documented gotcha — the world may have changed since the last session (inventory, prices, availability), and stale embedded results will be presented as if they're current. A structured summary plus a fresh state lookup is the recommended approach instead.

choices.text: The re-embedded listings may be stale — prices, availability, or inventory may have changed since yesterday, and presenting them as current risks misleading the user
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is a directly documented gotcha — for a returning user, re-embedding stale tool output risks presenting outdated information as current; a fresh state lookup should be paired with a structured summary instead.

choices.text: There's no risk; prior session tool output remains accurate indefinitely and never needs refreshing
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this directly contradicts the documented gotcha, which specifically warns that the world may have changed since the last session.

choices.text: The only risk is increased token cost, not staleness
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: while re-embedding does add tokens, the documented, more significant concern is presenting stale information (prices, availability) as if it were current.

choices.text: The only risk is that this violates the stateless core principle by remembering across sessions
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: re-embedding prior context across sessions doesn't violate statelessness itself (the app is explicitly resending content, which is consistent with the stateless model) — the documented concern is specifically about the staleness of that re-embedded content.

choices.text: There is no risk as long as the re-embedded content is labeled with yesterday's date
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: even with a timestamp, presenting stale listing data without a fresh lookup still risks the user acting on outdated prices or availability — the documented fix is a fresh state lookup, not just labeling.

choices.text: The risk only applies if the user is searching for real estate specifically
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this staleness risk applies generally to any returning-user scenario involving data that can change between sessions (inventory, prices, availability), not just real estate specifically.

stem: A team stuffs a 90K-token document into the middle of a long context window, reasoning that since the model has a large context window, every part of the input will be attended to equally. Key details from the middle of that document are frequently missed in the model's responses. What's the explanation, and what mitigation fits?
explanation: A large context window does not mean every token gets equal attention — models process content most reliably near the beginning and end; middle content is more likely to be under-weighted. Mitigations include placing key summaries/instructions at the top, using explicit section headers, trimming verbose content, and splitting into multiple focused passes when one pass can't reliably hold everything.

choices.text: Context capacity doesn't mean equal attention — middle content is under-weighted; mitigate by placing key info near the top/end, using section headers, or splitting into focused passes
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented "lost in the middle" gotcha and its mitigations exactly — the assumption that a large window guarantees equal attention is explicitly flagged as wrong.

choices.text: This is unexpected and indicates a bug; a large context window guarantees equal attention to every token
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is precisely the wrong-answer premise the guidance calls out — context capacity does not equal uniform attention.

choices.text: The fix is to increase max_tokens so the model has more room to process the middle content
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: max_tokens governs output length, not how reliably the model attends to input content positioned in the middle of a large context.

choices.text: The fix is to switch to the Batch API, which processes middle content more reliably
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: batch versus real-time is a latency/cost tradeoff unrelated to attention patterns across a large context window.

choices.text: The fix is to lower the temperature to 0, which eliminates the lost-in-the-middle effect
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: temperature affects output sampling randomness, not the documented positional attention pattern across a long context.

choices.text: There is no documented mitigation; this is an unavoidable limitation with no workaround
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the guidance explicitly documents several mitigations — top/end placement, section headers, trimming, and splitting into multiple passes.

stem: A single research pass is asked to reconcile 40 lengthy source documents at once, well within the model's technical context limit, but the resulting synthesis noticeably misses details buried in the middle documents. What's the recommended fix, rather than simply enlarging the context window further?
explanation: When one pass genuinely can't hold everything reliably, the recommendation is to split into multiple focused passes instead of enlarging the context window and hoping — since enlarging the window doesn't fix the underlying attention pattern ("lost in the middle"), only capacity.

choices.text: Split the reconciliation into multiple focused passes, since enlarging the context window doesn't fix the underlying attention pattern, only raw capacity
choices.reasoning: Correct: this matches the documented mitigation exactly — when one pass can't reliably hold everything, splitting into multiple focused passes is the recommended fix, not simply enlarging the window further.

choices.text: The fix is always to enlarge the context window further, since more capacity always solves attention problems
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is exactly the wrong-answer premise the guidance warns against — larger capacity doesn't guarantee equal attention to middle content.

choices.text: The fix is to increase max_tokens for the output, giving the model more room to write about the middle documents
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: output token budget doesn't address how reliably the model attends to and processes middle-positioned input content.

choices.text: The fix is to randomly shuffle the order of the 40 documents before each pass
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: shuffling doesn't address the underlying attention pattern — content in the middle of whatever the current order is will still tend to be under-weighted; the documented fix is splitting into multiple focused passes.

choices.text: The fix is to remove section headers so the model reads the documents more fluidly as one continuous block
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is the opposite of the documented mitigation — explicit section headers are recommended to make structure easier to locate, not removed.

choices.text: There is no fix beyond accepting the missed details as an inherent limitation
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the guidance explicitly documents splitting into multiple focused passes as an effective fix for exactly this situation.
